tldr: We present Norm2Tex, a plug-in method for vision-based tactile simulation. Without rebuilding high-density 3D meshes, it reconstructs fine surface bumps from normal maps and adds them to intermediate depth maps, reproducing realistic tactile textures with minimal computational overhead.
hero_caption: Comparison among real-world DIGIT sensor images (top), standard Taxim simulator outputs (middle), and Norm2Tex-augmented images (bottom). Standard simulators yield uniform, smooth contact images regardless of the material. In contrast, Norm2Tex faithfully reproduces fine tactile textures like wood grain, fabric weave, 3D printing layers, and rough stone.
overview:
Vision-based tactile sensors—which monitor the deformation of a soft gel membrane with an internal camera—are powerful devices. They capture not only overall object geometry but also micro-scale surface textures at the fingertip. However, training deep robot policies requires massive amounts of data, and repeatedly gathering physical contacts on real hardware is both time-consuming and expensive.

While tactile simulators are promising alternatives, most conventional simulators calculate contact deformation strictly from coarse 3D polygon meshes. As a result, high-frequency surface textures like fabric weaves or wood grain are completely lost, leading to a severe visual and feature discrepancy (Sim-to-Real gap). Conversely, modeling fine sub-millimeter or micro-scale bumps directly as 3D polygon meshes causes collision detection costs to skyrocket.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed Norm2Tex, a drop-in extension that integrates seamlessly into existing depth-map-based tactile simulators. Using procedural generation (mathematical rules and noise), it creates normal maps, reconstructs pseudo-height maps via Poisson integration, and directly adds them to the sensor depth maps generated during contact.

Experiments show that integrating Norm2Tex into existing simulators like TACTO and Taxim incurs almost no frame rate penalty (only about 1.5% rendering overhead on GPU). Furthermore, a classification model trained purely on simulated images achieved a 72% zero-shot material classification accuracy on real-world images, and a reinforcement learning policy trained to regulate grasping force successfully adjusted its actions in the real world based on material friction.
contributions: Proposed Norm2Tex, a lightweight plug-in method that integrates into existing depth-map-based tactile simulators with almost no computational overhead.
Built a procedural texture generation pipeline in Blender that automatically generates diverse normal maps by tuning noise and parameters, which can be applied to arbitrary 3D meshes.
Integrated the method into two representative simulators, TACTO and Taxim, and quantitatively verified that the impact on rendering speed is minimal.
Demonstrated successful Sim-to-Real transfer using simulation-only training on a zero-shot material classification task and a real-robot grasping force regulation task via reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: What Tactile Simulations Were Missing: Fine-Grained Surface Feel
sections.summary: While vision-based tactile sensors provide high-density signals, collecting real training data is challenging. Although simulators are expected to bridge this, current tools only account for coarse polygon geometry and miss surface textures. Norm2Tex solves this problem by using normal maps.
sections.details:
Vision-based tactile sensors, such as DIGIT and GelSight, point a small camera toward a soft silicone contact membrane, capturing its deformation during contact as RGB images. These images contain not only low-frequency information, such as overall tilt and contact curvature, but also rich high-frequency textures like roughness or wood grain. Such details are indispensable for slip detection, material classification, and defect identification.

However, training robot control policies requires huge amounts of contact data. While third-person external cameras can record continuously during robot motion, tactile sensors produce informative signals only at the exact moments of physical contact. Performing thousands of real-world contacts is prohibitively expensive, making simulated data generation highly desirable.

Unfortunately, most existing tactile simulators compute elastomer deformation solely from 3D object meshes. If one tries to model fine real-world surface textures as mesh vertices, the polygon count explodes and contact physics breaks down. Consequently, simulated contact images look like smooth, featureless plastic, creating a severe Sim-to-Real gap.

Norm2Tex tackles this problem not by building a separate standalone simulator, but as a drop-in extension that injects high-frequency textures into intermediate depth maps. As long as an object has a normal map, realistic tactile textures can be fed into the rendering pipeline without increasing mesh complexity.

sections.heading: From Contact Mechanics to Deep Generative Models: How Norm2Tex Differs
sections.summary: Vision-based tactile simulators range from direct depth-rendering models to physical FEM/MPM approaches. While GANs and diffusion models have been explored to bridge the texture gap, they require real data and lack temporal consistency. Norm2Tex operates between physics simulation and rendering, ensuring spatial consistency via UV mapping.
sections.details:
### Taxonomy of Vision-Based Tactile Simulators
Existing simulators model contact deformation through various paradigms. Early GelSight simulators, Taxim, and TacSL synthesize RGB images directly from contact depth using Phong reflection models or data-driven calibration maps. More recently, TacIPC and DiffTactile employ the Finite Element Method (FEM), while the Tacchi family uses the Material Point Method (MPM) to simulate internal elastomer stresses and marker displacements with high fidelity.

Norm2Tex targets the intermediate representation—the depth map—produced after contact mechanics calculations and right before final optical rendering. Because of this, it adds fine surface textures without complicating the expensive FEM or MPM contact physics. It occupies an orthogonal and complementary role to existing physics simulation techniques.

### Comparison with Prior Work in Texture Generation
To make simulated tactile images look closer to real ones, generative methods using image-to-image translation models like CycleGAN and SightGAN, or recent diffusion models like Tactile Diffusion, have been explored.

However, these deep learning approaches face two major challenges. First, they ultimately require collecting large volumes of real tactile data for training or fine-tuning. Second, they lack spatial and temporal consistency across consecutive frames. When a robot slides or drags across a surface, inconsistent bump patterns disrupt slip detection. In contrast, Norm2Tex directly couples with the 3D mesh geometry and UV-mapped normal maps, requiring zero real-world data while guaranteeing continuous, geometrically consistent observations.

sections.heading: From Normal Maps to Height Maps: Fast Frequency-Domain Poisson Integration
sections.summary: Norm2Tex first generates normal maps from procedural materials in Blender. It then converts them into pseudo-height maps using a fast Fourier-domain Poisson solver. During simulation, it crops the relevant region based on contact UV coordinates and adds it to the base sensor depth map.
sections.details:
### III-A Preliminaries: Handling Normal Maps
A normal map stores surface normal vectors in tangent space as RGB values in $[0, 1]$. Rescaling and normalizing them to $[-1, 1]$ recovers the surface normal vector $\mathbf{n}$. From this vector, we estimate gradients $h_x, h_y$ of the unknown height field along the $x$ and $y$ axes.

### III-B Texture Generation for Arbitrary Meshes
Because standard 3D assets found online often contain only RGB diffuse textures, the authors developed a procedural generation pipeline using Blender. By combining noise functions and structural parameters, normal maps and UV-unwrapped meshes for various materials—such as wood, fabric, rock, and 3D-printed surfaces—can be automatically synthesized.

### III-C Normal-to-Height Map Conversion (Poisson Integration)
To recover the surface relief (pseudo-height map) from the generated normal map, Norm2Tex uses Poisson integration in the frequency domain (Fourier domain) based on the Frankot-Chellappa algorithm. The normal map is divided into $N$ patches across UV islands, minimizing the least-squares error between the discrete gradient $\mathbf{d}_p$ and height map differences:

$$\min_{H_p} \sum_{i,j} (D_x(h) - d_{x,i,j})^2 + (D_y(h) - d_{y,i,j})^2$$

Setting the partial derivatives to zero yields the discrete Poisson equation $\Delta_d H_p = \nabla_d \cdot \mathbf{d}_p$. Assuming periodic boundary conditions, the problem is diagonalized in the frequency domain via the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). This allows instant height map recovery $H_p$ through an inverse FFT without solving linear equation systems.

Furthermore, reconstruction is carried out in two stages: a fine pass preserving microscopic bumps (Gaussian filter $\sigma=0.35$) and a coarse pass capturing gentle undulations ($\sigma=1.1$). Blending these with a weight $\alpha=0.2$ creates a realistic global height map $H_{\text{global}}$ offline.

### III-D Querying the Height Map at Runtime
During simulation, contact UV coordinates are determined from the relative pose between the sensor and the object computed by the simulator. The corresponding region is cropped from $H_{\text{global}}$ to yield a local height map $H_{\text{local}}$. Scaling this with a bump magnitude factor $\beta$ (e.g., 0.5 mm) and adding it to the baseline sensor contact depth $H_{\text{sensor}}$ yields:

$$H_{\text{final}} = H_{\text{sensor}} + \beta H_{\text{local}}$$

Passing $H_{\text{final}}$ to the existing simulator's renderer produces a tactile image where fine surface irregularities realistically affect lighting and shadows.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of Norm2Tex. Offline, Blender generates normal maps and a global height map $H_{\text{global}}$ from procedural textures. At runtime, a local height map $H_{\text{local}}$ is cropped using the contact surface's UV coordinates and added to the sensor depth $H_{\text{sensor}}$ in a simple, streamlined pipeline.

sections.heading: Experiments: Preserving Simulation Speed and Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
sections.summary: Integration tests with TACTO and Taxim revealed negligible impact on simulation speed. A ResNet-18 trained purely on simulated images achieved 72% accuracy classifying materials on real DIGIT images. Furthermore, an RL grasping policy successfully adapted its grip force based on material friction in the real world.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulator Compatibility and Computational Overhead
Norm2Tex was integrated into MuJoCo environments with Taxim and TACTO (depth-based pipeline), and the average rendering time over 1,000 frames was measured. Adding Norm2Tex introduced barely any latency. On a CUDA-enabled GPU, rendering time for Taxim increased by only 1.5%, proving its lightweight nature suitable for reinforcement learning data collection loops.

### IV-B Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Material Classification
To test whether simulated textures aid real-world perception, a 5-class material classification task was conducted (fabric, rock, smooth acrylic, 3D print, and wood). While 100 real images per category were collected using a physical DIGIT sensor, 6,000 simulated contact images per class were generated using Blender-tuned textures.

A ResNet-18 trained solely on simulated images achieved a 72% zero-shot accuracy when evaluated on real-world images. The confusion matrix revealed that faint layer lines on 3D-printed parts were sometimes confused with acrylic or wood, and deformable fabric was occasionally misclassified as rock. Nevertheless, it substantially outperformed random guessing (20%), confirming that texture cues directly facilitate Sim-to-Real transfer.

### IV-C Zero-Shot Grasping Force Regulation Policy
For dynamic control, an RL task was evaluated where a robot hand must hold a cube using the minimal grasp force (widest gripper opening) without dropping it. Slippage varies with the material's coefficient of friction, which can be inferred from surface texture. A 500 ml water bottle was suspended from the cube as a payload.

Evaluating policies trained via PPO showed that a blind baseline and a texture-free Taxim policy opened to a fixed gripper width regardless of material, dropping the object. In contrast, the policy trained with Norm2Tex retained an appropriate grip width for high-friction wood and fabric while holding more firmly on slippery acrylic, reproducing material-adaptive control on real hardware in zero shot.

captions.F4: Confusion matrix for zero-shot material classification on real-world data (left) and input images after subtracting the sensor's unpressed background (right). Rock, wood, and fabric achieve high accuracy, though slight confusion occurs between smoother acrylic and 3D-printed surfaces.
captions.F5: Wood texture images from Norm2Tex (top) and real DIGIT (bottom), along with their 2D Fourier transform spectra. Norm2Tex clearly captures the directional high-frequency components of wood grain. While real hardware attenuates high frequencies due to noise, the simulated signal is accurate enough to support classification and control.
captions.F8: Time-series trajectories of gripper opening width during the cube-holding task. The Blind and standalone Taxim policies converge to identical widths regardless of material, whereas Norm2Tex (bottom) demonstrates clear adaptive behaviors tailored to wood, acrylic, and fabric on the real robot (orange curve).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Work: Toward More Realistic Tactile Simulation
sections.summary: Norm2Tex shows that injecting normal-map-derived bumps into depth maps adds realistic textures to vision-based tactile simulations at minimal cost. Future directions include integration into FEM/MPM physics simulators and accurately capturing contact boundary shadowing.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Norm2Tex, a plug-in method that enriches vision-based tactile simulations with high-frequency surface textures using normal maps. By injecting height variations directly into the intermediate depth map without altering the underlying physics engine or mesh files, realistic contact images are produced while preserving existing rendering pipelines.

Models trained purely on simulated data reached 72% accuracy on real-world material classification and enabled material-dependent grasping behavior in robot control. These results strongly support the importance of texture signals in Sim-to-Real transfer.

Future work includes integrating this logic into advanced simulators based on FEM (Finite Element Method) or MPM (Material Point Method), as well as modeling the complex contact boundary shadows and optical artifacts that occur when real silicone pads are compressed. The texture generation pipeline will be released as open source.

takeaways: High-frequency textures can be added to tactile simulations with negligible computational overhead using normal maps and frequency-domain Poisson integration, avoiding dense 3D mesh subdivisions.
Because it functions as a plug-in that adds texture height to intermediate depth maps, it can be dropped directly into existing simulators such as Taxim and TACTO.
Surface textures in vision-based tactile images enable indirect inference of frictional properties, making advanced material-adaptive closed-loop control transferable from simulation to reality.
limitations: Simulators do not reproduce the characteristic shadows and optical distortions (artifacts) that appear around contact boundaries under deep silicone compression, causing discrepancy on subtle textures like acrylic.
Real tactile images often suffer from high-frequency attenuation due to sensor noise, meaning their frequency spectra do not perfectly match the crisp textures in simulation.
Currently, the pipeline does not physically couple bulk object deformation (e.g., fabric wrinkling or bending) with local texture distortion.
